title: Fluctuation electrodynamics of quantum capacitance in electron bilayers
authors: Dmitry Zverevich, Alberto F. Morpurgo, Alex Levchenko
abstract: Capacitance is a thermodynamic probe of interacting electrons: it measures the energy cost of moving charge between conductors, and in low-dimensional systems this cost is shaped by exchange and correlation as much as by electrostatics. We develop a theory of the quantum capacitance of electron double layers, semiconductor quantum wells as well as monolayer and bilayer graphene devices, focusing on the contribution generated by interlayer correlations. Within a functional-integral formulation we show that the separation-dependent part of the ground-state energy is, at the level of ring diagrams, exactly the nonretarded Lifshitz expression for the van der Waals energy of two conducting sheets, with reflection amplitudes built from the layer polarizabilities. The interlayer correction to the inverse capacitance is the second density derivative of this energy: a Casimir compressibility. The zero-point fluctuations that generate Casimir forces between mirrors are here the coupled plasmons of the bilayer, and their contribution to the capacitance is obtained in closed form, with a universal coefficient; its sign shows that interlayer correlations oppose charging at high density. A Gell-Mann-Brueckner analysis gives the exact high-density limit in terms of universal functions. For graphene we find that monolayers follow the electron-gas template, while bilayer graphene is anomalous: interband screening suppresses the correction by orders of magnitude and reverses its sign in the experimentally relevant range of separations. We delineate the limits of the theory, identifying the dilute Wigner-crystal regime and electron-hole double layers near exciton condensation as regimes where the capacitance becomes a probe of interlayer pairing.
summary: This paper develops a comprehensive theory for the quantum capacitance in electron bilayers by treating interlayer Coulomb correlations. It shows that these correlations manifest as a Casimir compressibility derived from coupled plasmon zero-point fluctuations. The work provides specific, material-dependent predictions, notably demonstrating anomalous screening effects in bilayer graphene.
main_problem: To develop a systematic theory for the quantum capacitance of electron double layers, specifically isolating and characterizing the contribution arising from interlayer Coulomb correlations.
main_result: The interlayer correlation to the inverse capacitance is shown to be equivalent to a Casimir compressibility derived from coupled plasmon zero-point fluctuations. For bilayer graphene, this correction is anomalous, exhibiting suppression and sign reversal in the experimentally relevant separation range.
method: The theory employs functional-integral formulations and ring diagram expansions (RPA generalization) to calculate the ground-state energy corrections due to interlayer interactions.
model_or_system: The primary model is two parallel 2D electron sheets (electron bilayers), applied to systems like doped monolayer and bilayer graphene. Interactions are mediated by the Coulomb potential, leading to coupled plasmon excitations.
key_observables: Quantum capacitance ($C$), inverse quantum capacitance ($\delta C^{-1}_{	ext{inter}}$), interlayer correlation energy, and Casimir compressibility.
important_parameters: Interlayer separation distance ($d$), electron density ($n$), and the ratio $k_F d$ (Fermi wavevector times separation).
main_assumptions: The calculation often assumes the nonretarded limit of the Lifshitz theory and neglects higher-order vertex corrections, though limits are defined for Wigner crystal or exciton condensation regimes.
figures_summary: Not specified in the notes; the focus is on deriving closed functional forms and asymptotic behaviors for the capacitance correction.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops the theory by first establishing the connection between interlayer energy and van der Waals/Casimir physics. It then applies this framework to specific materials (2DEG, graphene) to derive quantitative results, concluding with a discussion of theoretical limits and regimes where pairing effects dominate.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous quantum electrodynamic description of correlation effects in low-dimensional conductors, linking macroscopic transport properties (capacitance) directly to fundamental vacuum fluctuation forces (Casimir effect).
